content: 1. Simple supportive therapy, when used alone, can improve self-esteem and activate the existing strengths of individuals diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD). 2. Specific psychotherapies for BPD often require sessions spanning several months or, as is common with personality disorders, several years. 3. Psychotherapy can be conducted either individually or in group settings. Group therapy, in particular, can facilitate the development and practice of interpersonal skills and self-awareness in individuals with BPD, although high dropout rates can pose a challenge. 4. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is derived from cognitive-behavioral techniques and emphasizes a dialectical process of exchange and negotiation between therapist and client, as well as between rational and emotional perspectives, and between acceptance and change. 5. DBT prioritizes treatment targets, with self-harm issues being addressed first. It also focuses on assertiveness, social skills, adaptive coping with distress and crises, and the identification and regulation of emotional reactions. 6. DBT is based on a biosocial theory of personality functioning, which conceptualizes BPD as a biological disorder of emotional regulation within a social environment perceived as invalidating by the patient. 7. Research has shown that DBT significantly reduces self-injury and suicidal behavior in individuals with BPD, surpassing the effects of usual or expert treatment. It is also better accepted by clients, although its additional efficacy in the overall treatment of BPD remains less clear. 8. Training nurses in DBT has been found to replace therapeutic pessimism with a more optimistic understanding and outlook. 9. Schema therapy, also known as schema-focused therapy, integrates cognitive-behavioral and skills-based techniques with object relations and gestalt approaches. 10. Schema therapy directly addresses deeper aspects of emotion, personality, and schemas, which are fundamental ways of categorizing and reacting to the world. 11. This therapy also emphasizes the therapeutic relationship, including a process called limited re-parenting, as well as daily life outside therapy and traumatic childhood experiences. 12. Schema therapy was developed by Jeffrey Young and became established in the 1990s. 13. Limited recent research suggests that schema therapy is significantly more effective than transference-focused psychotherapy, with half of individuals with BPD achieving full recovery after four years and two-thirds showing clinically significant improvement. 14. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most widely used and established psychological treatment for mental disorders but has shown less success in BPD due to difficulties in establishing a therapeutic relationship and maintaining treatment adherence. 15. Approaches like DBT and schema-focused therapy were developed to expand upon traditional CBT, which typically involves a limited number of sessions targeting specific maladaptive patterns of thought, perception, and behavior. 16. A recent study found sustained benefits of CBT, in addition to treatment as usual, after an average of 16 sessions over one year. 17. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), a treatment for PTSD, is closely associated with BPD in many cases. EMDR shares similarities with CBT but includes unique techniques aimed at facilitating full emotional processing and resolving traumatic memories. 18. Marital therapy can stabilize relationships and reduce conflict and stress, which may exacerbate BPD symptoms. 19. Family therapy or psychoeducation can educate family members about BPD, improve communication and problem-solving, and provide support for dealing with their loved one's illness. 20. Two patterns of family involvement—overinvolvement and neglect—can guide clinicians in planning family interventions. 21. Traditional psychoanalysis is less commonly used today, both in general and for BPD, as it has been linked to symptom exacerbation. However, certain techniques have shown effectiveness in partial hospitalization contexts. 22. Transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), rooted in Otto Kernberg's concepts of BPD, involves an active therapist role and focuses on the patient-therapist relationship to clarify underlying object relations dyads. 23. Limited research suggests TFP may reduce some BPD symptoms by addressing underlying processes and improving reflective functioning and attachment security. 24. TFP has been shown to be as effective as DBT in reducing suicidal behavior and more effective in alleviating anger and reducing verbal or direct assaultive behavior. 25. Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT) combines cognitive and psychoanalytic approaches and has been adapted for BPD with mixed results. 26. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been shown in randomized controlled trials to improve symptoms of anxiety, depression, anger, and hostility associated with BPD in some patients. 27. Treating mood disorders associated with BPD often requires higher doses of SSRIs than treating depression alone, with benefits taking about three months to appear. 28. Atypical antipsychotics are claimed to have an improved adverse effect profile compared to typical antipsychotics and are sometimes used to treat distortions in thinking or false perceptions in BPD. 29. Long-term use of antipsychotics is controversial due to adverse effects, including tardive dyskinesia and significant weight gain with associated health complications. 30. Combining psychotherapy and medication is common in practice, but there is limited data on its clinical efficacy. 31. Challenges in BPD therapy include maintaining therapeutic relationships, addressing interpersonal sensitivity, and managing high dropout rates in medication trials. 32. Comorbid disorders, particularly substance use disorders, can complicate treatment and remission efforts.
